How to use

  • Diffuse 4 drops through an afternoon that needs lifting.
  • Blend with lavender and geranium for a softer floral citrus.
  • Keep diluted skin applications off areas exposed to sun — see below.

Dilute before applying to skin and patch-test first. Not for internal use.

Scent profile

  • Green citrus
  • Bitter rind
  • Soft floral

What's in it

  • 100% cold-pressed Citrus bergamia peel oil

Who it's for

Earl Grey drinkers

This is the scent in the tea, and recognising it is usually the moment bergamot clicks for people.

Anyone bored of lemon and orange

Far more complex than either — green and faintly bitter rather than simply sweet.

Evening diffusing

Bright without being stimulating, which makes it one of the more flexible citrus oils.

What people get wrong

Putting it on skin before going out. This is the single most important thing to know about bergamot. The reaction needs sunlight, so it can happen hours after application and leave marks that last months.

Assuming all bergamot is phototoxic. FCF or bergapten-free bergamot has had the reactive compounds removed and is safe in daylight. Ours is the cold-pressed, unrectified oil, which is not.

What it won't do

Like all cold-pressed citrus oils it has roughly a year in it from opening, and oxidised bergamot is both flatter and more likely to irritate skin.

We describe how our oils smell and how people use them. We don't make medical claims, because essential oils aren't medicine.

Questions about Bergamot

What does phototoxic actually mean?

Bergapten in the oil reacts with UV light on skin, which can cause burning and lasting dark patches. It needs both the oil and sunlight, so a blend applied in the evening and washed off is a different proposition from one applied before a walk.

What dilution is safe on skin?

Below 0.4% on any skin that will see daylight within about twelve hours — that is roughly one drop in four teaspoons of carrier. For diffusing, phototoxicity is not a concern at all.

Is this FCF bergamot?

No. FCF has the bergapten stripped out, which makes it daylight-safe but also removes some of the character. We sell the full cold-pressed oil and tell you how to use it.

How long does it keep once opened?

About a year. Cold-pressed citrus oils oxidise faster than distilled ones, and an oxidised citrus oil is both flatter to smell and more likely to irritate skin.

What dilution should I use on skin?

Lower than most. Phototoxic. Bergapten in cold-pressed bergamot reacts with sunlight — keep below 0.4% on skin that will be exposed, or use after dark. For general use, dilute into a carrier oil such as jojoba and patch-test on a small area first.

Can I take it internally?

No. None of our oils are food grade and none are sold for internal use. Essential oils are extremely concentrated, and advice to add them to water or food is not advice we endorse.
